currentUse: Probable identification: the former St. Casimir Lithuanian church building at 283 E 14th Street, Chicago Heights, IL is standing and used by a non-Catholic congregation; International Pentecostal Assemblies Ecumenical lists that address as its office (site copyright 2020), and Global True Lithuania reports a non-Catholic church operating inside a building surrounded by empty lots, with the Lithuanian name still carved in the cornerstone.
summary: Research indicates the only Lithuanian parish dedicated to St. Casimir (Šv. Kazimiero) in the Chicago area was in Chicago Heights, a south suburb — not in Marquette Park or Brighton Park as the archive record guessed; genealogical registers of Chicago-area Lithuanian parishes list St. Casimir only at Chicago Heights (genmetrika.eu), with the church/school building at 283 E 14th Street. Global True Lithuania reports the Lithuanian parish closed in 1987, that the two-story building (which housed both church and school and never gained a purpose-built second church) still stands surrounded by empty lots, that a non-Catholic church now operates inside, and that the Lithuanian name remains carved in the cornerstone. International Pentecostal Assemblies Ecumenical gives 283 E 14th Street, Chicago Heights as its address (site copyright 2020), consistent with the non-Catholic reuse. The stained-glass repatriation in the archive record is corroborated by a Bernardinai.lt article of 2013-08-14: ten roughly 90-year-old windows from a closed Chicago Lithuanian church bearing the name of Lithuania's patron saint, each originally donated by a Lithuanian family, arrived at the Vilnius Archdiocese restoration and construction trust around 2008, were cleaned, soldered and reinforced, were tentatively (but without signature or documentation) attributed to Adolfas Valeška by the Church Heritage Museum director, and as of 2013 were still awaiting a permanent home, with plans to adapt them to a newly built church. No later source documenting their final installation was found, and no sale price, buyer, diocesan closure decree, preservation campaign, or reunion activity for the parish property was found.

historicalNarrative.text: The Lithuanian St. Casimir institution represented by this public profile was in Chicago Heights, not within the City of Chicago and not in Marquette Park or Brighton Park. Two genealogical research guides independently place the Lithuanian parish in Chicago Heights, and the Chicago-area church index lists no second Lithuanian St. Casimir parish in the city. This geographic adjudication keeps the institution distinct from Polish and other same-name Catholic parishes.

historicalNarrative.text: The parish register guide identifies St. Casimir as a Lithuanian Roman Catholic parish and preserves online register coverage for 1911–1915. Its history places the church-and-school complex at 283 East 14th Street. These records establish early twentieth-century institutional activity and the Chicago Heights site without relying on a similarly named parish elsewhere.

historicalNarrative.text: The Lithuanian heritage survey describes the 14th Street property as a two-story structure that combined church and school functions; it says the parish never completed a separate purpose-built second church. The same field account reports that the Lithuanian parish closed in 1987. Because no diocesan decree or final-worship record has been located, that date remains an attributed closure reading rather than proof of the exact canonical mechanism.

historicalNarrative.text: Ten stained-glass windows associated in Lithuanian reporting with a closed Chicago-area Lithuanian St. Casimir church reached a Vilnius Archdiocesan restoration trust around 2008. Bernardinai reported in 2013 that the windows had been cleaned, soldered, and reinforced but still lacked a permanent home. Their attribution to artist Adolfas Valeška was explicitly tentative because the windows were unsigned and undocumented, and the source church was not identified by a full name-and-address statement. The object history is therefore preserved with that residual provenance uncertainty.

historicalNarrative.text: The former parish institution and the later use of its building are separate. International Pentecostal Assemblies Ecumenical lists 283 East 14th Street as an organizational address, while the heritage survey reports a non-Catholic congregation using the standing former church-and-school building and notes that the Lithuanian name remains on the cornerstone. This supports probable religious reuse of the historic property, not institutional succession from the Roman Catholic Lithuanian parish, and it does not establish the building's interior or structural condition.

developments.headline: Ten stained-glass windows arrive in Vilnius
developments.detail: Per a 2013 Bernardinai.lt report, ten stained-glass windows from a closed Chicago Lithuanian church bearing the title of Lithuania's patron saint (St. Casimir) arrived at the Vilnius Archdiocese restoration and construction trust about five years before the article — roughly 2008. The windows were described as about 90 years old, each with a Lithuanian family as donor.

developments.headline: Restored windows still seeking a permanent home
developments.detail: Bernardinai.lt reported the ten windows had been cleaned, soldered and strengthened; the Church Heritage Museum director suggested attribution to painter/stained-glass artist Adolfas Valeška (who founded a Chicago stained-glass studio in 1950-51), but the windows are unsigned and undocumented, and their ~90-year age sits awkwardly with that attribution. The plan discussed was to adapt them into a newly constructed church rather than an existing one. No later source confirming final placement was found.

conflictsWithArchiveRecord: ADJUDICATED 2026-07-27 (issue #89), verdict: CONFIRMED — no Lithuanian St. Casimir parish existed within Chicago city limits; the record's referent is the Chicago Heights parish (founded 1911, first Mass Easter April 21, 1912; closed 1987 per Global True Lithuania / 1989 per Wolkovich Vol 3 p. 147 — 'ceased in 1989, transferring its records to the archdiocesan archives'; variance carried, not resolved). Wolkovich Vol 3's comprehensive Illinois coverage (48 rows) lists exactly one Lithuanian St. Casimir parish: Chicago Heights. The record's own Draugas citations never place a parish in Chicago: 2013-08-20 is an Alkas.lt wire reprint saying only 'Prieš kelerius metus Čikagoje buvo uždaryta lietuvių Šv. Kazimiero bažnyčia' (loose locative, no neighborhood); 2013-09-07 is a reader letter disputing the Valeška window attribution (no location); 2017-12-12 is a St. Casimir Lithuanian Cemetery burial notice; 2017-05-06 is a biographical anecdote about the 1890s. The 'Marquette Park/Brighton Park (probable)' note was the case-file compiler's guess — the case-file itself flags 'precise neighborhood unstated'. The Bernardinai 'Mexican congregation' tension is RESOLVED in favor of Chicago Heights: Wolkovich documents Mexican parishioners there from 1948 and Spanish Augustinian pastors 1957-1966. City correction (Chicago → Chicago Heights) queued upstream; the locked CSV row is unchanged in this repo, and the registry sibling record st-casimir-chicago-heights-il is cross-referenced for upstream merge. || Original 2026-07-16 finding, confirmed by the adjudication: The archive's location note 'Marquette Park/Brighton Park area (probable)' appears to be wrong: genealogical registers of Chicago-area Lithuanian parishes (genmetrika.eu, lithuaniancatholicancestorsearch.com) show the only Lithuanian St. Casimir parish in the area was in Chicago Heights, a south suburb; Marquette Park's Lithuanian parish was Nativity BVM and Brighton Park's was Immaculate Conception. The Marquette Park association likely stems from the Sisters of St. Casimir motherhouse at 2601 W Marquette Road (mentioned in Draugas's 2015 heritage guide), a convent, not a parish. Archive's 'closed pre-2013' is consistent but refined: Global True Lithuania dates the closure to 1987. The '10 stained-glass windows repatriated' claim is corroborated by Bernardinai.lt (2013), with refinements: they arrived in Vilnius around 2008, are ~90 years old, tentatively but unverifiably attributed to Adolfas Valeška, and were still unplaced as of August 2013. One unresolved tension: Bernardinai describes the source church as closed 'a few years' before 2013 with a Mexican congregation worshipping there, which fits the 1987 Chicago Heights closure poorly — a Polish St. Casimir parish in Chicago's Little Village (merged into Our Lady of Tepeyac around 1990, Mexican congregation) also exists, so the windows' source church is not conclusively the Lithuanian Chicago Heights parish.
gaps: Narrowed 2026-07-27: the window-source-church doubt (Lithuanian Chicago Heights vs the Polish Little Village St. Casimir) is substantially reduced — Draugas/Alkas describe a LITHUANIAN church with a Lithuanian-family donor on every window, and Wolkovich's documented ethnic succession at Chicago Heights (Mexican parishioners from 1948) accounts for the 'Mexican congregation' detail — but the source church is still not documented by name-and-address in any opened source, so it remains a residual caveat rather than a closed question. Remaining gaps from 2026-07-16: The full Bernardinai.lt article is behind a Cloudflare block (HTTP 403; no Wayback snapshot exists), so its details come from search-engine excerpts of the article rather than the opened page — the most important verification gap in this record. The identity of the church the ten windows came from is not conclusively established (Lithuanian Chicago Heights vs. the Polish St. Casimir in Chicago's Little Village). No source was found for: the property's sale (price, buyer, year) after the parish ended; any Archdiocese of Chicago closure decree or official record (the archdiocesan closed-parishes PDF returned 403); the founding year of the parish; the final placement of the ten windows after 2013 (searched Lithuanian press for installation in a new church, including Vilnius Pilaitė St. Joseph — nothing found); any preservation campaign, recent press, or reunion activity. Searched in English and Lithuanian under 'St. Casimir', 'Šv. Kazimiero', 'Chicago', 'Chicago Heights', 'vitražai', and the 283 E 14th Street address.
